876.title: Seek, do, teach (Ezra 7:10)
876.hook: Ezra the scribe set his heart to seek the law, do it, and teach it
876.carry: study begins as a direction you set inside
876.howItsDone: A sofer is a trained Jewish scribe who writes Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot by hand with a quill and ink on parchment, following detailed laws for every letter, and Ezra is remembered in Jewish tradition as Ezra the Scribe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the new foundation, the sons of Asaph played, the old men wept, and the crowd shouted, and no one could tell the sounds apart. Your line was weeping and joy together. Did two feelings arrive at once? Day eight hundred seventy-six.

The book that bears his name runs for chapters before Ezra himself walks in. When he does, the text slows down to introduce him properly: a long line of fathers, name after name, back to Aaron the chief priest. Then, a job title. In the King James words: "he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD God of Israel had given." He comes up from Babylon with the king's permission and a company of returning exiles, and the text says the good hand of his God was upon him. Then it gives one sentence about what he set his heart on.
screen: `A LINE OF FATHERS, BACK TO AARON.` → `A READY SCRIBE.` → `UP FROM BABYLON.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments." Three verbs, in an order. Seek. The Hebrew verb is lidrosh, to search, to ask. Some readers hear in it the word midrash, the old Jewish way of searching a text for more than its surface. Ezra doesn't just read the law; he goes looking in it. Do. Before he teaches anyone, he does it himself. The verse puts the doing first, before a single word of teaching reaches anyone else. Teach. Only then does it go outward, to the people. And notice where it starts: he prepared his heart. Not his pen, not his scroll. Study begins as a direction you set inside. Today's word is what he was: a sofer, a scribe. The word is still in use. A sofer is the scribe who writes a Torah scroll by hand, letter by letter, with a quill on parchment, and tradition asks that a scroll for public reading be written that way, by someone who sits down and sets their heart to it.
screen: then, large: `SEEK IT, DO IT, TEACH IT.` · `DO IT BEFORE YOU TEACH IT.` · `HE PREPARED HIS HEART.` · then: `A SOFER STILL WRITES BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to study, do and teach one thing. Sit, and let your breathing settle. First, seek: take one line you trust, today's verse from Ezra if you like, or one from a book you keep near. Turn it over. Ask it one question. Second, do: find one way you could live it today, small and specific. Third, teach: think of who you could pass it to, and how you'd say it in a sentence. Seek, do, teach, in that order. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for a prepared heart. The bell holds the time.
Sofer. A scribe. Ezra was called a ready scribe in the law of Moses, and a sofer today still writes the Torah by hand. Today's word.
Your line: study begins as a direction you set inside. Today, live your one line once before you tell anyone about it, then pass it on. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

877.title: A quick prayer, then speak (Nehemiah 2:1–5)
877.hook: the king's cupbearer prays silently, then makes his request
877.carry: the slow work was done before
877.howItsDone: Jewish tradition has set prayers for fixed times, and also short, personal prayers said in the moment; Nehemiah's silent prayer before answering the king is sometimes pointed to as an example of the second kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezra the sofer, the scribe, set his heart to seek the teaching, do it, and teach it. Your line was study begins as a direction you set inside. What did you pass on to someone? Today, a different man in a different job: he pours the king's wine. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

A cup of wine is on its way to a king. The man carrying it is Nehemiah, a Jew in exile, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia, in the palace at Shushan. He stands close enough for the king to read his face, and he says he had never been sad in the king's presence before. But Nehemiah has heard news from home: the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned with fire. He wept, the book says, and fasted, and prayed. Now he hands over the cup, and the king looks at him and sees it. Why is your face sad, the king asks, when you aren't sick? This is nothing but sorrow of heart. Nehemiah writes that he was very much afraid. And then comes a moment that lasts about as long as a breath.
screen: `THE KING'S CUPBEARER.` → `NEWS FROM HOME: THE WALL IS DOWN.` → `THE KING SEES HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Nehemiah answers honestly. Let the king live forever; why shouldn't my face be sad, when the city where my fathers are buried lies waste and its gates are burned? Then the king asks the question everything turns on. In the King James words: "For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And the very next words: "And I said unto the king." That's the whole prayer, in the text. No kneeling, no long speech, no time. The king is waiting, the cup is in the room, and between the question and the answer Nehemiah prays. The book doesn't tell us the words. It doesn't need to. What it shows is the order: a quick prayer, then speak. Notice this isn't his only prayer. In chapter one he prayed at length, with fasting and confession and a long plea. So the quick prayer stands on top of a long one. The slow work was done before; the short prayer is what fits in the gap. Then Nehemiah speaks, and he's specific. If it please the king, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may build it. He goes on to ask for letters for safe passage and for timber from the king's forest. And the king grants it, the text says, according to the good hand of God upon him. A prayer that fits in a breath, then a clear, concrete ask. Today the king might be a manager, a doctor, a landlord, a parent. The gap between their question and an answer is short. Nehemiah shows what can fit inside it.
screen: `AN HONEST ANSWER TO THE KING.` · then, large: `SO I PRAYED TO THE GOD OF HEAVEN.` · `A LONG PRAYER CAME FIRST.` · then: `A CLEAR, SPECIFIC ASK.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to pray a breath, then ask. Sit, and let your hands rest. Bring to mind one request you need to make soon: a raise, a day off, help with something, an apology you're hoping for, a hard conversation. See the person you'll ask. Hear them say, so what is it you want? Now take one breath in the gap. If you pray, you can turn to God in that breath, silently, in your own way or with words from your tradition. If you don't, let the breath steady you. Then, in your mind, say the ask plainly, in one or two sentences, the way Nehemiah did. The bell holds the time.
cupbearer, Nehemiah's role serving King Artaxerxes, the position he held when he prayed a quick prayer and then spoke. Today's word.
Your line: the slow work was done before. Today, before one important answer, take a single breath first, then say clearly what you need. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

what a scholar hears: the short prayer rests on a long one in chapter one, and the book is written in Nehemiah's own voice: "so I prayed."

878.title: Build anyway (Nehemiah 4:11)
878.hook: the wall is rebuilt with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other
878.carry: one hand on the stone, one hand ready
878.howItsDone: Some Jewish readers turn to Nehemiah's builders, working with one hand and guarding with the other, as a picture of carrying on with a community's work under threat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nehemiah stood before the king and fit a whole prayer into one breath. Your line was the slow work was done before. Did you take the breath before you answered? Today, he arrives in Jerusalem, and the work begins. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

First come the jokes. Nehemiah has reached Jerusalem, rallied the people, and they've started raising the wall on its old lines, family by family, each beside its own stretch. Across the way stand the local strongmen, Sanballat and Tobiah, and they laugh. In the King James words, Sanballat sneers, "What do these feeble Jews?" And Tobiah adds that if a fox went up on what they're building, it would break their stone wall down. The jokes don't stop the work. So the jokes turn into threats: a plan to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause trouble. Now the builders have a choice. Stop until it's safe, or find a way to keep going.
screen: `THE WALL GOES UP ON ITS OLD LINES.` → `FIRST THE MOCKERY.` → `THEN THE THREATS.`

segments.voice: Nehemiah does two things at once, and the text puts them side by side: "Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night." Prayer and a guard, together. Then he reorganizes the whole site. Half the young men work, half stand ready. Behind every section are the people's leaders. And here is the picture this day is named for. The verse is numbered eleven in Hebrew Bibles and seventeen in the King James, and it reads: "every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon." One hand on the stone. One hand ready. The builders wear swords at their sides while they lay brick. A man with a shofar, a ram's horn, stands next to Nehemiah, and the plan is simple: wherever you hear the horn, gather to us there; our God will fight for us. They work from the first light until the stars come out. Nehemiah writes that he and his men didn't even take off their clothes, except for washing. They don't wait for the threats to go away. They don't pretend the threats aren't real either. They hold both: the danger in one hand, the work in the other. Earlier, the text gives the reason the wall kept rising at all: the people had a mind to work. A hard week, a project people laugh at, a goal someone wants to stop: the wall in Nehemiah was built by people with only one hand free.
screen: `PRAYER AND A WATCH, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HAND GUARDS.` · `GATHER WHERE THE SHOFAR SOUNDS.` · then: `THE PEOPLE HAD A MIND TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to keep building under pressure. Sit, and rest your hands on your knees, palms up. Let the right hand hold something you're building: a project, a family, a habit, a piece of work that matters. Let the left hand hold whatever is pushing against it: doubt, criticism, tiredness, a real worry. Don't drop either one. Just feel both hands and breathe. Then ask: what is one brick I can lay today, even with this in my other hand? Keep that one small task in mind. If you pray, you can bring both hands to God, the way Nehemiah's builders prayed and kept watch. The bell holds the time.
Build anyway. The wall of Jerusalem goes up with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, because the people had a mind to work. Today's word.
Your line: one hand on the stone, one hand ready. Today, lay one brick on something that matters to you, even if a worry is still in your other hand. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

what a scholar hears: the book holds prayer and practical defense together, "we made our prayer... and set a watch", and never treats one as a replacement for the other.

879.title: They gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:1–8)
879.hook: the people stand as Ezra reads, and Levites explain so everyone understands
879.howItsDone: In synagogue services the Torah is read aloud from the scroll, and teaching that explains the reading, through a sermon, a study session or a translation, is a familiar part of Jewish communal life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wall went up with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. Your line was one hand on the stone, one hand ready. What brick did you lay? Today the wall is up, and the people gather to hear something read. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

The request comes from the crowd. In the King James words, all the people gathered themselves together as one man into the street that was before the water gate. And they speak to Ezra the scribe, the same Ezra who set his heart to seek, do and teach. Bring out the book of the law of Moses, they say. So Ezra brings it before the whole congregation, men and women, and everyone old enough to understand. He climbs a wooden platform built for the purpose, high enough to be seen. He opens the book in front of them all. And when he opens it, the text says, all the people stand up. But a book read aloud isn't the same as a book understood. That's where this chapter turns.
screen: `THE PEOPLE ASK FOR THE BOOK.` → `EZRA ON A WOODEN PLATFORM.` → `THE BOOK OPENS. EVERYONE STANDS.`

segments.voice: Ezra blesses the LORD, and the people answer, Amen, Amen, lifting up their hands, then bowing with their faces to the ground. He reads from early morning until midday, and the text says the ears of all the people were attentive. Then comes a detail that's easy to skip. Standing beside Ezra is a list of named men, and with them the Levites, and their job is to help the people understand the teaching while the people stand in their places. Then the verse this day is named for: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Three steps. They read it distinctly, clearly, not rushed. They gave the sense: they explained what it meant. And they caused them to understand. The goal isn't that the words were said. The goal is that the people got it. The text doesn't tell us exactly how the Levites did this, whether they moved through the crowd, or translated, or taught in small groups; readers have suggested each of these. What it does say is that reading alone wasn't counted as enough. There were people standing between the words and the listeners, building a bridge. A form, a diagnosis, a contract, a hard text: the words can all be there and still not land. What helps is the person who sits down and says, here's what this means. That's what the Levites did in the street before the water gate.
screen: `AMEN, AMEN, HANDS LIFTED.` · `LEVITES BESIDE THE READER.` · then, large: `READ DISTINCTLY. GAVE THE SENSE.` · then: `SAID ISN'T THE SAME AS UNDERSTOOD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to explain something clearly. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Think of one thing you understand that someone near you doesn't yet: how something works at your job, a recipe, a rule of a game, a line of a text you love. Now picture explaining it to them. First, say it distinctly, in plain words, slowly. Then give the sense: what does it actually mean, why does it matter? Then check: would they understand it now? Trim one word you don't need. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for clear speech and patient listening. The bell holds the time.
Sekhel. Ezra reads, the people stand, and the Levites explain until the reading is understood, with sekhel, good sense. Today's word.
Your line: gave the sense. Today, when you explain something, don't stop at saying it; stay until the other person has it. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: Joy is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10)
880.hook: "the joy of the LORD is your strength"; eat, drink and send portions
880.howItsDone: Jewish festivals are kept with festive meals, and on Purim it is the custom to send gifts of food to friends and give to the poor, as the book of Esther describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezra read the teaching at the water gate, and the Levites gave the sekhel, the sense, so everyone understood. Your line was gave the sense. Who did you help understand something? Today, what the people do once they understand. Day eight hundred eighty.

The crowd is crying. All morning they've stood in the street and listened, and now that the words have been explained, they finally understand them. And understanding hits hard. The text says it plainly: all the people wept when they heard the words of the law. Maybe they're hearing how far they've drifted. Maybe it's the weight of a whole people coming home. The book doesn't say why. It only says they wept. And then their leaders do something unexpected. Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites don't tell them to cry harder. They tell them to stop.
screen: `THE WORDS ARE UNDERSTOOD.` → `ALL THE PEOPLE WEEP.` → `THE LEADERS SAY: STOP.`

segments.voice: This day is holy to the LORD your God, they say; don't mourn, and don't weep. Then comes an instruction that sounds like a party invitation. In the King James words: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our LORD: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength." Look at what's packed in there. Eat the rich food. Drink the sweet drink. And send portions to the people who have nothing ready. The joy isn't private. It goes out the door on a plate. Then the line this day is named for: the joy of the LORD is your strength. The Hebrew word for strength here is ma'oz, and some readers hear in it a stronghold, a place of refuge. On that reading, the picture isn't only a feeling of being strong; it's a place to stand. Joy as a wall, in a book about building walls. The Levites quiet the people: hold your peace, for the day is holy; don't be grieved. And the people go off to eat and drink and send portions and make great rejoicing, the text says, because they had understood the words that were declared to them. That last phrase ties yesterday to today. The tears came from understanding, and so did the joy. Nehemiah's instruction for a holy, happy day is to set a table and fill a second plate. Readers of the book of Esther may hear an echo here: Purim, too, is kept with feasting and with sending portions one to another.
screen: `THIS DAY IS HOLY. DON'T WEEP.` · `EAT, DRINK, SEND PORTIONS.` · then, large: `THE JOY OF THE LORD IS YOUR STRENGTH.` · then: `JOY BECAUSE THEY UNDERSTOOD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to share food on a good day. Sit, and let your face soften. Bring to mind one good thing from this week, small or large. Let yourself actually enjoy remembering it. Now think of someone for whom nothing is prepared: a neighbor who eats alone, a friend having a hard month, a coworker who skips lunch. Decide on one portion you could send them: a meal, a snack, a coffee, a plate from your own table. See yourself handing it over. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
Joy is your strength. The people stop weeping, eat and drink, and send portions to those with nothing, because the joy of the LORD is their strength. Today's word.
Your line: joy is your strength. Today, when something good happens, send a portion of it to someone who has nothing prepared. Day eight hundred eighty.

881.title: From Adam (1 Chronicles 1)
881.hook: the Tanakh's last book begins with Adam and a list of generations
881.howItsDone: Jews read Chronicles as part of the Writings, the third section of the Tanakh; Jewish families also keep track of lineage in ways such as naming children after relatives and recording family names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people stopped weeping and sent portions to those with nothing prepared. Your line was joy is your strength. Who got a second plate from you? Today, we open the book that closes the Tanakh. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

Three names, and no introduction. In the King James words, the book begins: "Adam, Sheth, Enosh." No "in the beginning", no setting, no verb. Just names, and then more names, generation after generation, chapter after chapter. This is Chronicles. In Hebrew it's called Divrei Hayamim, the words, or the events, of the days. In the order of books the Talmud lists, it comes last of all, so the Hebrew Bible, which opened with Adam in Genesis, comes back around to Adam at its end. A page of names can look like the part to skip. Today, let's not skip it.
screen: `ADAM, SHETH, ENOSH.` → `DIVREI HAYAMIM: THE EVENTS OF THE DAYS.` → `THE LAST BOOK STARTS AT THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Chronicles retells the whole story, and it starts by compressing everything from Genesis into lists. Adam to Noah. Noah's sons. Abraham. Isaac. Jacob, whom the book calls Israel. Then the tribes, one by one, with their families and towns. Why begin like this? A list of names says something a story can't say as quickly: nobody here came from nowhere. Every person stands at the end of a long line. And the lists aren't as dry as they look. Tucked into the names of Judah's family is a man called Jabez. His mother, the text says, named him that because she bore him in pain. Then, in the middle of the list, Jabez calls out to God, asking to be blessed and kept from harm, and the text says God granted what he asked. One small prayer, buried in a genealogy, as if to say every name on this page had a life and a voice. Now look where the lists end up. After all the generations, the book arrives at the people who came back from exile and settled again in Jerusalem, people like the ones we've just been reading about in Ezra and Nehemiah. So the chain runs from Adam to the returned exiles. One way to read that opening: the people rebuilding a small city after exile are placed inside a story as wide as humanity. A life can be lived as if it started with itself. Chronicles opens with a list that says otherwise.
screen: `GENESIS SQUEEZED INTO LISTS.` · then, large: `NOBODY CAME FROM NOWHERE.` · `JABEZ: A PRAYER IN THE LIST.` · then: `FROM ADAM TO THE RETURNED EXILES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to trace your family back one step. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Say, silently, the name of someone who raised you or whose family you come from. It might be a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an adoptive family, anyone who handed life on to you. Now go one step further back. If you know the name of their parent, say it. If you don't, that's fine; let the space stand for someone real whose name is simply out of reach. Rest there, at the end of a long line. If you pray, you can remember them in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
From Adam. Chronicles, last in the Talmud's order of books, opens with Adam and walks the generations down to its own day. Today's word.
Your line: from Adam to now. Today, ask someone older one name from your family you've never heard, or write down one you know. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

882.title: Let him go up (2 Chronicles 36:23)
882.hook: the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's call to go up and rebuild
882.howItsDone: In synagogue, being called up to say the blessings over the Torah reading is called an aliyah, a going up, and moving to the land of Israel is also called making aliyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chronicles opened with three names: Adam, Sheth, Enosh. Your line was from Adam to now. Did you find a name in your family line? Today, the last page of that same book, and the last words of the Hebrew Bible. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

The second-to-last scene is a ruin. At the end of Second Chronicles, the Babylonians burn the house of God, break down the wall of Jerusalem, and carry the survivors away to Babylon. The text says the land lay desolate and kept its sabbaths, as the word of the LORD by Jeremiah had said. If the book stopped there, the whole Hebrew Bible would close on smoke and exile. It doesn't stop there. Two more verses come. A new king rises, Cyrus of Persia, and he sends out a proclamation through all his kingdom, in speech and in writing. And in the order this path follows, the last word of the whole Tanakh is a verb of movement.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF GOD BURNED.` → `THE PEOPLE CARRIED TO BABYLON.` → `THEN CYRUS SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the final verse, in the King James words: "Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD God of heaven given me; and he hath charged me to build him an house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? The LORD his God be with him, and let him go up." And there it stops. In Hebrew, the very last word is ve-ya'al: and let him go up. Eight days ago we heard this same decree open the book of Ezra, and there the sentence keeps going: let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD. Chronicles stops one breath sooner. No Jerusalem yet, no building, no arrival. Just a question, who is there among you, a blessing, and the first step of a road. In the order this path has been following, the Hebrew Bible ends mid-sentence, with the destination left off the page. Some readers hear in it the word aliyah, a going up: being called up to the Torah in synagogue is called an aliyah, and so is moving to the land of Israel. Now look back at this week. Ezra set his heart: study begins as a direction you set inside. Nehemiah said: the slow work was done before. The builders kept one hand on the stone, one hand ready. The Levites gave the sense. The people learned that joy is their strength. Chronicles reached from Adam to now. And the whole library closes on let him go up. A week of rebuilding, and it ends not with the building done, but with the call to keep climbing.
screen: `WHO IS THERE AMONG YOU?` · then, large: `LET HIM GO UP.` · `EZRA GOES ON; CHRONICLES STOPS.` · then: `A WEEK OF REBUILDING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to take one step upward. Sit tall, as if a thread were lifting the top of your head. Breathe in, and feel the spine lengthen. Now hear the question Cyrus asks: who is there among you? Let it be a question to you. Think of one place in your life where you've been stuck in the ruins a while: something left broken, put off, given up on. Choose one step up from there, one small enough to take today. A call, a page, a clean-up, a first try. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for help to go up. The bell holds the time.
Ve-ya'al. And let him go up: the last words of the Hebrew Bible, Cyrus's call to the people, and let them go up and rebuild. Today's word.
Your line: the call to keep climbing. Today, take the one small step up you chose, before the day ends. Day eight hundred eighty-two.
